lessons.title: Management information systems on the farm
lessons.html:
From records to a management information system

At N6 level the farm manager is responsible not just for records and analysis but for the whole system that delivers information to decision-makers: a management information system (MIS). An MIS combines people, procedures, data and technology so that the right information reaches the right person at the right time, in a usable form.

Components of a farm MIS

  • Data sources – field records, weighbridges and scales, milk meters, weather stations, soil moisture probes, GPS yield monitors, payroll, accounting systems, buyer statements.
  • Storage – databases or cloud platforms with defined structures, rather than scattered spreadsheets.
  • Processing – calculations, summaries, indicators and models.
  • Outputs – reports, dashboards, alerts and exports for lenders, auditors and buyers.
  • People and procedures – who captures, checks, approves and uses the data.

Information needs by level

LevelTypical information
Owner / boardProfitability by enterprise, return on assets, cash position, risk exposure, multi-year trends
Section managersWeekly production against plan, costs per unit, labour productivity, quality results
SupervisorsDaily task lists, targets, stock on hand, exceptions such as sick animals or breakdowns

Database concepts

Relational databases store data in linked tables: for example an Animals table (one row per animal, unique tag ID), a Weighings table and a Treatments table, each linked by tag ID. Benefits include no duplication, consistent data, and the ability to query across records, such as all heifers treated in the last 30 days that are below target weight. Key concepts are the primary key (unique identifier), foreign key (link to another table), validation rules and controlled lists of values.

Selecting software

When choosing farm management or ERP software, evaluate fit to enterprises, ease of field capture (offline mobile use is important where signal is poor), integration with accounting and equipment, reporting, data ownership and export, vendor support, security and total cost of ownership.

lessons.title: Data governance, quality and decision support
lessons.html:
Data governance

Governance defines who owns, may access and is accountable for each set of data. Without it, data becomes inconsistent, insecure and untrusted.

  • Assign data owners (e.g. the livestock manager owns herd data).
  • Define standard codes and names: block numbers, camp names, product names, cost centres.
  • Set role-based access: who may view, capture, edit, approve and delete.
  • Keep audit trails of changes.
  • Define retention periods and backup and recovery procedures, and test them.

Legal and market requirements

Personal information of employees, customers and suppliers must be processed lawfully, for a specific purpose, kept secure and limited to what is needed, under the Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013. Market access programmes such as retailer and export food safety standards require traceability: the ability to trace a product forward to customers and back to the field, inputs and workers involved. Chemical application records, animal identification and movement records are frequently audited.

Data quality dimensions

DimensionQuestion
AccuracyDoes the value reflect reality?
CompletenessAre required values present?
TimelinessIs data available when needed?
ConsistencyDo the same items agree across systems?
ValidityAre values in the allowed format and range?

Monitor these with exception reports, such as missing daily milk records or weights outside plausible ranges, and fix root causes in capture procedures.

Decision support

Well-managed data supports advanced tools: precision agriculture (variable-rate fertiliser from yield maps and soil sampling grids), herd genetic evaluation, forecasting of yields and cash flow, and scenario models that test price, yield and cost assumptions. Key performance indicator dashboards should focus on a few measures linked to strategic goals and show trends and targets. Managers must still apply judgement: models depend on assumptions, and correlation in historical data does not prove cause.

Key points

  • An MIS links people, procedures, data and technology to deliver decision information.
  • Different management levels need different information.
  • Relational databases link tables by keys to avoid duplication and enable queries.
  • Governance sets ownership, standards, access, audit trails and backups.
  • Comply with POPIA and traceability demands; monitor data quality dimensions.
